stimulus.text: In July 1775, the Second Continental Congress sent the Olive Branch Petition to King George III. The petition affirmed loyalty to the king and blamed the troubles on Parliament, proposing that the colonies govern themselves more freely within the empire. George III rejected the petition without reading it. Historians estimate that about 40 to 45 percent of colonists were Patriots who wanted independence, about 15 to 20 percent were Loyalists who wanted to keep ties with Britain, and the rest did not strongly support either side.

books.section: B. Common Sense, the Declaration of Independence, and Republican Self-Government

stem: What does the Olive Branch Petition show about the Second Continental Congress in July 1775?

options.text: That Congress had already voted for independence and was stalling for time
options.misconception: Congress voted for independence a year later, in July 1776 — in July 1775 it was still seeking reconciliation.

options.text: That Congress refused to negotiate with Britain under any terms
options.misconception: The petition is itself a negotiation — Congress offered the king a settlement, it did not refuse to talk.

options.text: That Congress blamed the king personally for every colonial grievance
options.misconception: The petition blamed Parliament, not the king — it affirmed loyalty to George III.

options.text: That most delegates still hoped for reconciliation rather than independence

rationales.D: The petition affirmed loyalty to the king and proposed self-government within the empire — reconciliation, not separation. In July 1775, mending the empire was still the aim.
rationales.A: Independence came a year later. In July 1775 Congress was still trying to mend the empire, not leave it.
rationales.B: The petition was an offer to settle. Refusing to negotiate would have meant sending nothing at all.
rationales.C: The petition blamed Parliament and affirmed loyalty to the king — the reverse of blaming George III.
rationales.general:
1. Read what the petition asks. Loyalty to the king, blame on Parliament, self-government inside the empire.
2. Ask what that means. Congress was offering reconciliation, not declaring separation.
3. Set the date. July 1775 is a year before independence — most delegates still hoped to mend the empire.
Remember: a petition for reconciliation tells you what its writers still wanted — read the ask, not the later outcome.
